newsitem.title: USA: FAA bomb detection training inadequate - NTSB.
newsitem.headline: FAA bomb detection training inadequate - NTSB.

text.p: The National Transportation Safety Board on Tuesday recommended new procedures for bomb-sniffing dog exercises aboard aircraft, saying current operations could inadvertently indicate that explosives were on a flight.

The NTSB concern arose after investigators discovered minute traces of explosive chemicals in the wreckage of TWA Flight 800 which were residue from a canine test conducted on the Boeing 747 six weeks before it crashed off Long Island last July 17.

During the investigation into the TWA disaster, the NTSB found that the Federal Aviation Administration dog handler worked alone rather than with a team, used "deteriotaed" explosive training aids whose containers were not intact, and failed to notify anyone about the trace amounts of explosives released.
The NTSB said the handler stated that he may also have spilled explosive material inside the aircraft cabin.
"Failure to report these spills led to confusion concerning the forensic evidence of explosives during examination of debris," the board said.

The NTSB noted that the FAA had since issued new procedures and standards, but said:"The Safety Board is concerned that (they) may not be sufficient to ensure the reliability and integrity of the K-9 explosives detection program and to eliminate all opportunities for inadvertent placement of explosive materials into the system and ultimately on a scheduled flight."
